Performance of microaeration hydrolytic acidification process in the
pretreatment of 2-butenal manufacture wastewater
Guangqing Songa,b,c, Yin Yua,c, Tao Liud, Hongbo Xia,c,⁎, Yuexi Zhoua,c,⁎
a Research Center of Water Pollution Control Technology, Chinese Research Academy of Environmental Sciences, Beijing, 100012, PR China
b College of Water Sciences, Beijing Normal University, Beijing, 100875, PR China
c State Key Laboratory of Environmental Criteria and Risk Assessment, Chinese Research Academy of Environment Sciences, Beijing, 100012, PR China
d School of Environmental and Municipal Engineering, Lanzhou Jiaotong University, Lanzhou, 730070, China
G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
2-Butenal manufacture wastewater
Microaeration hydrolytic acidification process
Organic loading rates
Extracellular polymeric substance
Microbial community
A B S T R A C T
The performance of the microaeration hydrolytic acidification (MAHA) process and microbial community were
investigated under different organic loading rates (OLRs) for the pretreatment of 2-butenal manufacture was-
tewater (2-BMW). Results indicated that OLRs had different impact on the performance of MAHA process. More
than 23.7 ± 2.3% of the chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal and the highest acidification degree
(20.9 ± 3.1%) were obtained when OLRs were less than 4.0 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d. However, further increasing
OLRs to 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d subsequently led to the significant reductions of COD removal and acidification
degree. In addition, it could be preliminarily inferred that 2H-pyran-2-one tetrahydro-4-(2-methyl-1-propen-3-
yl), 5-formyl-6-methyl-4,5-dihydropyran and ethyl sorbate were the main refractory and toxic organics for
microorganisms in the wastewater. The soluble microbial product (SMP) and extracellular polymeric substance
(EPS) contents (protein, polysaccharide, nucleic acid) had obvious changes under different OLRs. With parallel
factor (PARAFAC) model, four fluorescent components were identified. The Fmax of protein-like substances in
SMP significantly decreased with increasing OLRs to 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d, which might attribute to fluor-
escence quenching. Illumina MiSeq sequencing revealed that Pseudomonas, Longilinea, T78, Clostridium, WCHB1-
05, Acinetobacter, SHD-231 and Oscillospira were dominant genera at different OLRs.

1. Introduction
2 -Butenal (also named crotonaldehyde) is an important industrial
chemical for synthesizing sorbic acid. Sorbic acid as food preservative,
which is recognized as safe substance in certain degree, has become one
of the most common preservatives in the food industry throughout the
world [1]. With increasing demand on sorbic acid, the yield of 2-bu-
tenal presents an increasing trend. In China, 2-butenal is mainly pro-
duced by aldehyde condensation technology [2]. With this production
technology, aldehyde, acetic acid and polymerization inhibitor are
needed during the production process, which leads to a toxic, refractory
and highly concentrated 2-butenal manufacture wastewater (2-BMW).
Untreated wastewater released directly into the biological treatment
processes could cause severe damage to microbial activity. At present,
the effective technologies for wastewater pretreatment have been rarely
reported in the literature. Thus, it is necessary to explore an efficient
and economical pretreatment process for 2-BMW.
Hydrolytic acidification (HA) is an economical and effective pre-
treatment way, which plays an important role in breaking refractory/
toxic organic matters and improving the biodegradability [3,4].
Therefore, HA process has been widely used in pretreatment field of
toxic and refractory wastewater [5]. However, hydrolysis is usually a
rate-limiting step for wastewater containing complex pollutants. To
solve this situation, some new methods for enhancing hydrolysis effi-
ciencies were proposed. Recently, literature reported that microaera-
tion was an alternative method to enhance hydrolysis of complex or-
ganic matter [6]. Under anaerobic conditions metabolites (lactic acid
and ethanol) are usually formed to oxidise nicotinamide adenine di-
nucleotide (NADH2). However, microaeration could effectively reduce
the formation of toxic metabolites and increase formation of the desired
products [7]. In addition, microaeration could help in the synthesis of
certain lipids that are required for the cellular growth [8]. Moreover,
the study of Charles et al. revealed that microaeration could enhance
the cellulase and protease exoenzyme activities [9]. Until now, micro-
aeration has been predominantly used for the desulphurization of
biogas [10]. Besides, some researches have examined the effect of mi-
croaeration on the solid waste anaerobic digestion [11,12]. However,
there are few research available with regard to the application of mi-
croaeration hydrolytic acidification (MAHA) process on the pretreat-
ment of industrial wastewater.
A lot of researches have been carried out on the effect of different
factors on anaerobic process rather than HA process. Organic loading
rate (OLR) is commonly reported to be a critical parameter in anaerobic
process. However, for 2-BWM, the effect of OLRs on the pretreatment
efficiency remains unknown with MAHA process. Obviously, the sta-
bility of reactor performance is susceptible to toxic shock from the
pollutants in 2-BWM. The toxic shock to microorganisms became
greater with increasing OLRs. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate
the effect of OLRs on the reactor performance for MAHA process. In
addition, it is reported that the production of microbial extracellular
polymeric substance (EPS) is considered to be an important self-pro-
tection strategy under unfavorable environment [13]. For example, Shi
et al. reported that granules produced more EPS with adding tetra-
cycline (TC), and TC caused EPS fluorescence spectroscopy quenching
[14]. Nevertheless, the effect of industrial wastewater on the change of
EPS content under different OLRs has been relatively less studied,
especially for the 2-BWM. The microbial community is crucial to im-
prove efficiency of biological treatment process. Several studies have
investigated the microbial community during HA process treating
dyeing wastewater [15], 2-BMW [16], and trimethylolpropane [17].
However, there is no related literature reporting the microbial com-
munity in MAHA process for 2-BMW.
The main objective of this work was to evaluate the effect of OLRs
on the bioreactors performance by HAHA process. Firstly, the effects of
OLRs on the bioreactor performance were investigated. Secondly, var-
iations of soluble microbial product (SMP) and the EPS contents and
fluorescence characteristics of EPS under different OLRs were analyzed.
Thirdly, microbial community structures with OLRs were investigated.
This study would provide reference for practical application of MAHA
process for the pretreatment of 2-BMW.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Main characteristics of 2-BMW
The wastewater used in this work was collected from the production
processes of 2-butenal in northern China. The physicochemical char-
acteristics of 2-BMW are as following: pH 3.8～4.3, chemical oxygen
demand (COD) 86,702～87,945 mg/L, biochemical oxygen demand
over five days (BOD5) 10,907～11,614 mg/L (BOD5 value was mea-
sured after wastewater dilution), total organic carbon (TOC) 29,101～
29,315 mg/L, alkalinity 230～257 mg/L as CaCO3, total dissolved solids
(TDS) 15,901～16,285 mg/L.
2.2. Experimental setup and inoculum
The expand granular sludge bed (EGSB) reactor was made of acrylic
plexiglass with an internal dimeter of 60 mm and height of approxi-
mately 1600 mm. The reactor was composed of reaction ozone (4.5 L)
and sedimentation ozone (4.8 L) (Fig. S1). The temperature was main-
tained at 37 ± 1 °C by a thermostatic waterbath. The hydraulic re-
tention times (HRT) was 24 h. The up-flow velocity (Vup) was kept
stable at 2.9 m/h by effluent recirculation with peristaltic pump. Air
was added continuously in the effluent tank by aerator pump, which
was carried into the EGSB reactor through effluent recirculation. The
microaeration of 0.2～0.5 mg/L was provided to the EGSB reactor. The
EGSB reactor was inoculated with 2.0 L anaerobic sludge, which was
obtained from the integrated petrochemical wastewater treatment
plant. The concentration of suspended solid (SS) and volatile suspended
solid (VSS) were 11.1 ± 0.5 g/L and 8.0 ± 0.3 g/L, respectively. The
volatile suspended solids to suspended solids (VSS/SS) of sludge was
0.72.
The influent COD was gradually increased by diluting 2-BMW.
NH4Cl and KH2PO4 were added in the wastewater as nitrogen and
phosphorus, respectively. The nutrient ratio (COD:N:P) used was
200:5:1.
2.3. Analytical methods
Analysis of COD, TDS, alkalinity and VSS were analyzed according
to the standard methods for the examination of water and wastewater
[18]. TOC-VCPH instrument (Shimadzu, Japan) was employed to mea-
sure TOC. The pH and oxidation reduction potential (ORP) were de-
termined by a portable meter (FE20, Mettler Toledo, Switzerland).
Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and identification of organic matters were
determined in accordance with previous reports [16].
2.4. EPS extraction and analysis
A heat extraction method was employed to extract SMP, loosely
bound-EPS (LB-EPS) and tightly bound-EPS (TB-EPS) from sludge
samples under different OLRs [19].
The polysaccharide (PS) content in SMP, LB-EPS and TB-EPS ex-
tractions was measured with phenol-sulfuric acid method [20]. The
protein (PN) content was determined using BCA protein kit (Sangon,
China). The nucleic acid (NA) content was measured using the diphe-
nylamine colorimetric method with sodium salt of calf thymus DNA as
the standard.
2.5. 3D-EEM fluorescence spectroscopy and PARAFAC analysis
Three-dimensional
excitation-emission
matrix
(3D-EEM)

466

fluorescence spectra of SMP, LB-EPS and TB-EPS extractions were ob-
tained using a luminescence spectrometry (F-7000, Hitachi, Japan). The
excitation wavelength (Ex) was set as 200～450 nm with emission
wavelength (Em) 280～550 nm.
Due to the complexity of SMP and EPS compositions, there was the
problem of significantly overlapped fluorescence spectra. Therefore,
parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis was adopted to separate the actual
fluorescence spectra from the 3D-EEM [21,22]. The spectrum of double
distilled water as blank sample was measured, and was deducted from
the 3D-EEM spectra of the samples. To eliminate the distractions of
Rayleigh scattering, the 3D-EEM data close to the Rayleigh scattering
line were set to zero [23]. The corrected fluorescence data were then
modeled with the DOMFluor Toolbox in Matlab R2009a [24]. The split-
half and residual analysis was further performed to validate the number
of fluorescence components [25]. The fluorescence intensity of each
component was represented by Fmax (R.U., i.e. Raman units) [26].
2.6. Microbial structure analysis
In this study, sludge samples were taken in the stable operation
phase with different OLRs. DNA was extracted from sludge samples
with Tiangen® soil DNA kit (Tiangen Biotech, China) following the
manufacture’s protocols. The extracts were stored at −20 °C before
further analysis. The V3-V4 regions of the 16 s rDNA genes were am-
plified with 340 F (CCTACGGGNBGCASCAG) and 805R (GACTACNV-
GGGTATCTAATCC). All polymerase chain reaction (PCR) reaction
mixture was purified with the MinElute Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen,
Germany). The Invitrogen™-Qubit fluorometer quantitative system
(California, USA) was used to quantity the amplicons. Then high-
throughput sequencing of 16S DNA amplicons were sequenced with the
Illumina MiSeq platform at SinoGenoMax Co., Ltd (Beijing, China).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performances of EGSB reactor under different OLRs
The reactor was ran continuously for 159 days and experienced
shock loading and recovery stage. Fig. 1 shows the reactor performance
in terms of COD, COD removal, pH, ORP, VFAs concentration and
acidification degree during the experiment.
As shown in Fig. 1 (a), OLRs increased gradually from 0.5 ± 0.1 to
6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d with influent COD increasing from 512 ± 25
to 6037 ± 111 mg/L at shock loading stage. To reactivate microbial
activity, OLR was then decreased to 4.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d corre-
sponding to influent COD 4082 ± 94 mg/L at recovery stage. The ef-
fect of different OLRs on the COD removal is displayed in Fig. 1(b). The
COD removal was 61.7 ± 5.6% at stage I. From stage II to VI, the COD
removal decreased steadily from 44.1 ± 4.5% to 23.7 ± 4.5% with
OLRs increasing from 1.1 ± 0.1 to 4.0 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3·d. However,
further increasing OLRs to 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d (stage VII), the COD
removal decreased sharply to 13.4 ± 1.8%. At recovery stage VIII, OLR
was decreased to 4.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3·d by reducing influent COD.
The COD removal quickly achieved 23.1 ± 1.1%. Comparatively, the
COD removal in the HA reactor remained less than 20% when OLR was
decreased to 4.1 kgCOD/m3 d after shock loading of 6.1 kgCOD/m3 d
[16].
The suitable pH and ORP values could provide good growing con-
ditions for microorganisms, so the above two parameters were mon-
itored in the course of the experiment [27]. The Fig. 1(c) depicts the
variations of pH and ORP under different OLRs. During stage I～II, the
effluent pH maintained 5.8～6.7 while the reactor interior ORP rapidly
lowered from −55 mV to −315 mV. The reactor created relatively
good circumstance for microorganisms. As increasing OLR (stage III),
the effluent pH decreased gradually from 6.1 to 5.1. This implies that
the reactor was not well self-buttered. Meanwhile, ORP increased
steeply from −322 mV to −239 mV. To resolve the above problems,
NaHCO3 as the alkalinity was added to influent for the following ex-
periment. After improving the influent alkalinity, the effluent pH soon
returned to normal and maintained in the range of 5.9～7.4 at stage IV
～VI. In addition, ORP lowed quickly to below −300 mV. Despite the
slight fluctuation of effluent pH and reactor interior ORP, the overall
performance of EGSB reactor was steady. However, further improving
OLRs, reactor interior ORP increased dramatically from −269 mV to
−79 mV, possibly due to the increase of inhibition and/or toxicity ef-
fects on microorganisms. Similar result has been found previously by
Blanc et al., who indicated that an increasing ORP correlated to in-
hibited or decreasing levels of digester performance [28]. At recovery
stage VIII, reactor interior ORP rapidly dropped to −340 mV with OLR
decreasing to 4.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d.
Fig. 1(d) shows the VFAs concentration and acidification degree
under different OLRs. Seven kinds of VFAs, including acetic, propionic,
n-butyric, n-valeric, n-hexanoic, 2-methyl butyric and 2-ethyl butyric
were detected in this study. However, the dominant fermentation pro-
ducts were acetic, n-butyric, and 2-ethyl butyric. The others VFAs were
produced in insignificant amounts. As shown in Fig. 1(d), no sign of
VFAs in the effluent was detected at stage I～II, which demonstrated
that fermentation products were metabolized by facultative bacteria in
the reactor. As can be seen in this study, as OLRs increased, the con-
centration of fermentation products appeared firstly increased and then
decreased during stage III～VII. With OLRs increasing from 1.6 ± 0.1
(stage III) to 4.0 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d (stage VI), the acidification degree
increased from −12.7 ± 1.0% to 20.9 ± 4.4%. However, further in-
creasing OLR to 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d (stage VII) subsequently led to
the significant reductions of acidification degree. The acidification de-
gree reduced from 15.6% to −1.5%, with the corresponding COD re-
moval dropping from 17.9% to 11.7%. The phenomenon indicated that
OLR of 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d caused the EGSB performance to
worsen. Ding et al. also reported that acidification degree began to drop
when OLR reached maximum, which was largely ascribed to in-
sufficient of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes [29].
3.2. Characterization of organic compositions
The organic compositions in the influent and effluent under dif-
ferent stages were analyzed by GC–MS. Fig. 2 depicts a representative
GC–MS chromatogram for influent and effluent at stage VI. As shown in
Fig. 2, the species and abundance of organic matters decreased con-
siderably by MAHA process. Twenty-three kinds of typical compounds
were detected in the influent, including aldehydes, alcohols, esters,
organic acids and phenols. The relative retention times of the first three
highest peak were 10.769, 14.772 and 15.507 min, corresponding to
2H-pyran-2-one
tetrahydro-4-(2-methyl-1-propen-3-yl),
5-formyl-6-
methyl-4,5-dihydropyran and ethyl sorbate, respectively.
Some new peaks (a～q) were displayed in Fig. 2 (b), and these new
organic matters could be correspond to hydrolytic intermediates and
microorganism metabolites, such as acetic acid, 2-pentanone, 2-methyl-
propanoic acid, butanoic acid, 3-methyl-butanoic acid, 2-methyl-buta-
noic acid, 2-ethyl-butanoic acid, hexanoic acid, 3-methyl-2,4-pentan-
diol,
3-methyl-3-hexen-2-ol, (E)-1-methoxy-4-hexene, 3-cis-hexenyl me-
thyl carbonate, cytosine, cis-3-hexenyl lactate, 2,4-dihydroxypyridine,
cis-2-hexenyl acetate, (E)-2-hexenoic acid. The removal efficiencies of
organic compounds at different stages are reported in Table S1. Most of
the organic matters could be hydrolyzed into more readily degradable
organic matters during stage I˜VI, which illuminates that the MAHA
process was capable of decomposing refractory and toxic organic
matters in 2-BMW. Nevertheless, most of compounds were not effec-
tively degraded at stage VII, including especially 2H-pyran-2-one tet-
rahydro-4-(2-methyl-1-propen-3-yl),
5-formyl-6-methyl-4,5-dihy-
dropyran and ethyl sorbate. The removal efficiencies of the above three
compounds were 65.2 ± 4.6%, 70.0 ± 6.1% and 68.5 ± 2.5%, re-
spectively. Because of a lack of commercial standard, the toxic effects

cular structure and literature.
3.3. Variations of SMP and EPS contents under different OLRs
Fig. 3 summarizes the variations of SMP and EPS (LB-EPS, TB-EPS)
contents (PN, PS and NA) under different OLRs. The variations of PN,
PS and NA in the SMP under different OLRs are shown in Fig. 3(a). With
the increase of OLRs, the PN content in the SMP generally increased
firstly and then decreased during stage I～VI. However, further increase
of OLR to 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d (stage VII), the PN content increased
sharply from 3.4 ± 0.1 to 13.5 ± 0.3 mg/gVSS. The PS and NA con-
tents had no obvious change rule during stage I～VI, whereas the PS
and NA content increased sharply from 2.7 ± 0.3 to 7.8 ± 0.3 mg/
gVSS and 1.4 ± 0.4 to 17.2 ± 0.9 mg/gVSS, respectively, at stage VII.
This result might be attributed to release of intracellular material which
was caused by toxic substance at stage VII (OLR 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/
m3 d). This phenomenon was similar to the one in literature reported by
Fukushi et al., that the PS and NA levels increased in the presence of
40 mg/L of Cu and Cd due to cell death and lysis [32].
The variations of LB-EPS and TB-EPS contents (PN, PS and NA)
under different OLRs are shown in Fig. 3(b) and (c), respectively. With
the increase of OLRs from 0.5 ± 0.1 to 2.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3·d, the PN

reducing trend with further increasing OLRs. This results showed that
high OLRs might not markedly promote the EPS production due to the

It is worth noting that PN content was dominant in EPS production,
revealing that PN played a more significant role in protecting cell from
the harsh external environment. The observation was also well reported
by Sheng et al., in which PN as the major component in EPS protected
against the harmful effects by diffusion limitation and/or by chemical
binding [35]. As OLRs increased, the NA content in the LB-EPS revealed
a general increase, while the NA content in the TB-EPS did not change
evidently.
3.4. PARAFAC analysis of 3D-EEM fluorescence spectra
The PARAFAC model of SMP and EPS from sludge samples under
different OLRs revealed that the fluorescence could be characterized by
four different components (Fig. 4(a)). Fig. 4 (a) also presents Ex/Em
loadings of the four components. Component 1 consisted of two ex-
citation maxima at 220 and 280 nm, with one emission peak centered at
355 nm. Component 1 resembled the typical aromatic protein (Ex/Em
220/355 nm) and soluble microbial byproduct-like matter (Ex/Em 280/
355 nm) [22]. Component 2 had the maxima loadings at Ex/Em wa-
velength of 225/305 nm and 265/305 nm, which were associated with
tyrosine-like fluorophore. Component 1 and component 2 had been
ascribed to protein-like fluorophores [36]. Component 3 had a primary
(secondary) fluorescence peak at an Ex/Em wavelength of 275(225)/
325 nm, which might be regarded as the blue shift of component 1.
Component 4 were characterized by excitation at 210, 240 and 320 nm,
and emission at 430 nm, which demonstrated the existence of UVA
humic-like substance [37].

showed the fluorescence intensity (Fmax) of the four components in
SMP, LB-EPS and TB-EPS samples as OLRs changed. The protein-like
substances (component 1, 2 and 3) were major constituents in SMP, LB-
EPS and TB-EPS samples. The Fmax of component 1, 2 and 3 generally
showed an increasing trend, which was inconsistent with the protein
content in SMP samples during stage I～VI. The increase in Fmax of
protein-like substances suggested that it played a certain role in the
organic matter removal and transform in biosorption process. Aquino
et al. investigated the interaction between protein-like substances and
chloroform, indicating that the accumulation of protein-like substances
increased as the amounts of toxic chloroform increasing [38]. Never-
theless, under OLR of 6.08 kgCOD/m3·d (at stage VII), the Fmax of SMP
samples showed a sudden drop, which was the opposite of the protein
content change at this stage. Possibly because the protein-like sub-
stances of SMP were obviously quenched with organic matters in the
wastewater. More detailed, the Fmax of component 1, 2 and 3 in SMP
was decreased from 1310, 1194 and 1351 at stage VI to 580, 161 and
365 at stage VII, respectively. Previous studies have reported that
protein-like substances as fluorophores was clearly quenched by phe-
nanthrene [39]. In this present study, the quenching mechanism about
fluorescence was not investigated due to intrinsic complexity of was-
tewater sample. Moreover, comparing to protein-like substances, the
Fmax of humic-like substance (component 4) had no evident change as
increasing OLRs, which was probably due to that the contents of humic-
like substances were lower than protein-like substances. Similar results
have been reported by Hou et al. [40].
The variation tendency of Fmax of component 1, 2 and 3 in LB-EPS
and TB-EPS was different from those in SMP, owing to the fact that LB-
EPS and TB-EPS are not susceptible to organic matters as they are less
close to 2-BMW than SMP. The Fmax of component 1, 2 and 3 increased
firstly and then decreased in LB-EPS and TB-EPS, which was consistent
with the variation of protein. Component 2 was the primary component
at stage I～VI in LB-EPS, which indicated that there existed a large
amount of tyrosine-like substance. The existence of tyrosine-like sub-
stance might be a useful emergency measure which was used to avoid
the adverse effects of organics in wastewater. For TB-EPS, there was no
evident regularity of different components. Su et al. also found that the
EEM spectra of the TB-EPS showed no obvious change due to TB-EPS
locating in the inner layer of the sludge floc [41].
3.5. Microbial community analysis
Illumina Miseq sequencing was used to analyze the V3-V4 region of
16 s rRNA of sludge samples for revealing the variation of microbial
community. The community richness and diversity indices of different
samples were shown in Table S2. The OTUs in the samples ranged from
1714 to 4095. The lowest OTUs of 1714 were obtained at stage VII,
which exhibited less richness of microbial communities than the one at
others stages. Ace and Chao indices indicated community richness,
while Shannon and Simpson indices represented community diversity
[42]. Ace, Chao and Shannon had significantly changed amount dif-
ferent samples, suggesting that OLRs had an important effect on the
microbial community diversity in MAHA reactor. In comparison, lower
indices of Ace, Chao and Shannon were achieved at stage VII, which
indicated that OLR 6.08 kgCOD/m3 d (stage VII) had a negative impact
on the community richness and evenness.
As shown in Fig. S2, principal component analysis (PCA) revealed
obvious separation of microbial communities at different OLRs. The
percentage variance of species explained by the first and second axis
was 35.59% and 17.99%, respectively. Seven samples were dispersed
into four distinct regions of clusters. The sample I and III grouped to-
gether, while the samples (II, IV and V) gathered together. They were

well separated from samples (VI and VII), but there was a clear dis-
tinction between sample VI and VII. The PCA results further demon-
strated that the microbial communities in MAHA reactor were impacted
by OLRs.
The diversities of microorganisms at the phylum and class level in
MAHA reactors were shown in Fig.5, in which the relative abundance of
two taxonomic levels (phylum and class) was greater than 0.6% in at
least one sample. As shown in Fig.5 (a), microbial community exhibited
similar diversities but obviously different abundance at the phylum
level. Proteobacteria (19.51～71.80%), Chloroflexi (9.27～37.06%),
Firmicutes (1.62～25.49%) and Bacteroidetes (3.59～15.41%) were
dominant phyla in all samples. These four phyla accounted for more
than 75% of the total bacteria in seven samples. Proteobacteria, Chlor-
oflexi, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes were reported to be dominant phyla
in hydrolytic acidification system for treatment of 2-BMW [16]. Pre-
vious research reported that Proteobacteria could degrade extensive
organic matters and existed widely in wastewater treatment [43]. At
stage VII (OLR 6.08 kgCOD/m3 d), the proportion of Proteobacteria
reached the maximum (71.80%). In comparison, Chloroflexi initially
accounted 37.06% at stage I (OLR 0.51 kgCOD/m3 d) and then de-
creased to 9.27% at stage VII (OLR 6.08 kgCOD/m3 d). The study of Lv
et al. revealed that Chloroflexi could degrade starch to acetate and other
short-chain fatty acids [44]. At stage VII, the 2-BMW had an adverse
effect on the microbial activity, ultimately resulting in a decrease in the
proportion of Chloroflexi. The phylum Firmicutes not only was a larger
participant in VFA generation, but also could secrete more endospores
to survive in the toxic environment [45,46]. Meanwhile, Bacteroidetes
were known to convert amino acids generated during protein hydrolysis
into acetate [47]. The relative abundance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes
generally appeared increase tendency as OLRs increasing. However, at
stage VII they showed a reducing trend, possibly due to the increase of
inhibition and/or toxicity effects on microbial activity.
Fig. 5(b) showed the relative abundance of bacterial community on
the class level. The dominant bacterial communities were Anaerolineae
(9.18～37.06%), Gammaproteobacteria (4.47～64.32%), Alphaproteo-
bacteria (4.40～26.80%), Clostridia (1.47～25.22%), Betaproteobacteria
(1.90～18.41%) and Bacteroidia (1.23～13.24%). Anaerolineae pre-
sented a prominent abundance in all the samples at different stages.
Nevertheless, the relative abundance of Anaerolineae has been sig-
nificantly decreased at stage VII. Notably, the relative abundance of
Gammaproteobacteria was obviously improved, whereas an opposite
tendency was shown in the abundance of Alphaproteobacteria, Clostridia
and Bacteroidia when OLRs varied from 4.04 to 6.08 kgCOD/m3·d.
The heatmap graph depicts the profiles of 50 most abundant genera
in samples with different OLRs (Fig. 6). There was substantial variation
of bacterial community among samples, which implied a great effect of
different OLRs on microbial community structure in MAHA process. As
shown in Fig. 6, eight major bacterial genera were detected in all
samples, namely Pseudomonas, Longilinea, T78, Clostridium, WCHB1-05,
Acinetobacter, SHD-231 and Oscillospira. Under OLRs less than 4.04
kgCOD/m3·d, the relative abundance of Pseudomonas was kept almost
stable. However, with OLRs increasing from 4.04 to 6.08 kgCOD/m3·d,
Pseudomonas abundance rose from 0.02% to 57.58%. It was reported
that Pseudomonas was bacterium with the capacity to degrade re-
fractory aromatic compounds [48], and could survive under the cir-
cumstance of high-cyanide [49], which suggested that Pseudomonas had
stronger resistant ability under strict condition. This might be the
reason why Pseudomonas abundance increased largely with the increase
of OLRs. Longilinea and Clostridium were hydrolysis fermentation and
acidogenic bacteria, which played important roles for hydrolysis and
acidogenesis during the course of the treatment [50]. The relative
abundance of Longilinea and Clostridium at stage VI accounted for
25.53% and 6.51%, respectively. This result was consistent with the
maximum acidification degree at stage VI. Due to higher OLR (stage
VII), Longilinea and Clostridium abundance showed evident decrease,
which indicated that the concentration of toxic contaminant at stage VII
could be deleterious to Longilinea and Clostridium. Oscillospira with
Firmicutes was reported to play a crucial role in food waste acidogenic
reactors [51]. Moreover, previous study indicated that Oscillospira was
vulnerable to sulfamethoxazole and its relative abundance decreased
with operation time [52]. For T78, there were few reports about its
exact role in previous literatures. The Oscillospira and T78 abundance
overall appeared first increase then decrease trend. In this study,
WCHB1-05 and SHD-231 were also detected under different OLRs.
According to Petropoulos et al., WCHB1-05 with high lipolysis was
often enriched in the absence of available organic material at low
temperature [53]. Meanwhile, the genus WCHB1-05 was associated
with the degradation of hydrocarbons [54]. SHD-231 was often ob-
served in wastewater, but its function was seldom mentioned. The re-
lative abundance of WCHB1-05 and SHD-231 showed decrease with
increasing OLRs in this study. Various studies have reported that Aci-
netobacter had potential ability to degrade toxic substances (3,5,6-tri-
chloro-2-phyidinol, azo dyes, et. al.) [55,56]. The abundance of Aci-
netobacter at stage VII was significantly more than those at other stages,
which confirmed that Acinetobacter might to be special genera corre-
lated to detoxification.
4. Conclusions
The MAHA process provided an efficient technique for the pre-
treatment of 2-BMW, but OLR of approximately 6.08 kgCOD/m3·d
would result in a failed performance of the reactor. Additionally,
GC–MS analysis results revealed that the refractory and toxic organics
in the 2-BMW could be hydrolyzed into more readily degradable or-
ganic matters when OLR was less than 4.04 kgCOD/m3·d. With regard
to the microbial community, Pseudomonas, Longilinea, T78, Clostridium,
WCHB1-05, Acinetobacter, SHD-231 and Oscillospira were dominant
genera. This study demonstrated that the MAHA process could be
